source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's NVA9 campus in Sterling, Virginia publishes 38 MW of IT capacity and 700,000 square feet of technical space, and ranks 16th among the 29 Virginia facilities that publish a megawatt figure.

The two published numbers describe different things. Megawatts measure the power the campus can deliver to servers, square feet measure the building that houses them. Neither converts into the other without an assumption about rack density that CyrusOne does not publish. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 38 MW is roughly 950 racks. At 10 kW per rack it is roughly 3,800. The rack count is ours, not the operator's, and should not be quoted as if it were a specification.

For AI specifically, the 38 MW figure is the binding one. Accelerators are limited by delivered power before they are limited by floor area, so a campus with 700,000 square feet of technical space and 38 MW of published capacity is a power-constrained asset, not a space-constrained one. That is the shape of the current buildout: land and shells are available, interconnection and generation are not.

The data does not say who occupies NVA9, what hardware runs there, or whether the site holds any certification for federal, financial, or health-data workloads. The certification field is empty, which means the spec page is silent, not that the campus is unqualified. Virginia's 2,563.4 MW total across 29 publishing facilities is likewise a floor. Most mapped Virginia sites publish no megawatt figure at all, so the state's real capacity is larger than any total this data can produce.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
